Box 11 Case studies: Voluntary cyber resilience centers (CRCs)

Los Angeles Cyber Resilience Center

The Port of Los Angeles launched its Cyber Resilience Center in January 2022 to serve

as a “system of systems” for rapid sharing of cyber threat indicators and collective

defense among terminal operators, shipping lines, rail, trucking, and other supply-chain

stakeholders. Building on the Port’s internal Cyber Security Operations Center (established

in 2014), the CRC centralizes and automates the exchange of cyber indicators and defensive

measures, offers training and tabletop exercises, and provides an early warning function

to protect cargo flow. The port’s board approved an agreement with IBM in late 2020 to

design, operate, and maintain the CRC, leveraging threat intelligence and orchestration

technologies.

2.2.3 Operationalizing Incident Response Using Security

Operations Centers

A Security Operations Center (SOC) is a centralized team that monitors, detects, and responds

to cyber threats in real time, and it is a critical element of incident management. Without

one, organizations may struggle to identify escalation channels, delaying or preventing

effective response.

Survey findings revealed an unexpected pattern. Middle-income countries were least likely to

operate an in-house or managed SOC, while high-income and low-income countries showed the

highest rates of SOC outsourcing. Yet interviews suggest an encouraging shift, with more low- and

middle-income port operators turning to third-party SOC services as a pragmatic way to build

capability where in-house expertise is limited. Clear reporting protocols across all staff are equally

pressures and the perceived absence of a compelling business case. These factors reduce investment

in cybersecurity controls, as such measures avert losses rather than produce measurable revenue.

Economic barriers arise when different parties do not share the same goals and problems spill over:

if one operator cuts back on cybersecurity, it can raise risks for everyone else, creating so-called

negative externalities. Some parties may be tempted to benefit from others’ investments without

contributing themselves, free-riding8 on others (Moore 2010). On top of that, information gaps make

it hard to assess risks clearly and learn from past events. This chapter examines these key barriers

to improving cybersecurity in ports and first discusses human capacity barriers (3.1), then financial

barriers (3.2), and finally economic barriers (3.3).
